Keys recovered via the same yellow fill-rectangle highlight and ad hoc PyMuPDF detection method lane 3 validated for this source, render-confirmed again this pass on page 30 (this dispatch's 1 available render; 0 mismatches across all 4 marks on that page, including 2 that print a responsibility/accountability definition reversed from conventional teaching -- render-confirmed as genuinely printed rather than a detection error, but held rather than authored this pass, deferred with the rest of page 30's non-selected items for topical-balance/scope reasons, not doubt in the mark itself). Of the roughly 106 detected question blocks across pages 12-40 (96 single-marked, 8 unmarked, 2 script-merge artefacts each resolved into two clean single-marked sub-items), this pass authors 47, selected for topical balance across all four sections and to avoid this source's own internal near-duplication (the bioethics-principles block is tested near-verbatim twice, pages 12-16 then 16-23) and duplication against lanes 1-3's existing 94 concepts (vertical equity, double effect, and genetic-factors-are-non-modifiable each recur here and are held rather than re-minted, named twin in each case). Two items (vulnerable-populations-except and modifiable-determinants-except) print 5 options in the source; kept at 5 rather than trimmed, since every option is a genuine, distinct list member and the module's >5-trimmed rule does not require reducing a clean 5-option set. questions.title: Definition of bioethics
questions.question: Bioethics: is

options.A: the research of ethical, social, and legal issues.
options.B: the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in biomedicine and biomedical research.
options.C: the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in life.
options.D: the study of science issues that arise in biomedicine and biomedical research.

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Research" names an activity bioethics may draw on, not the definition of the field itself, and it drops the biomedicine-specific scope the source marks as essential.
explanations.B: Correct. Bioethics is defined here as the study of ethical, social and legal issues that specifically arise in biomedicine and biomedical research. This scopes the field to medicine and medical research rather than to life or society in general, which is exactly the distinction the source draws against the other options. It is this biomedicine-specific framing that makes this option, and not the broader or narrower alternatives, the one the source marks correct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Issues that arise in life" broadens the definition beyond biomedicine and biomedical research, which is the scope the source specifically names.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option drops "ethical" and "social" from the scope, narrowing bioethics to only science issues, which does not match the source's three-part definition.

questions.learning_objective: State that bioethics is the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in biomedicine and biomedical research.

questions.title: Bioethical concepts
questions.question: Bioethical concepts are

options.B: Persons without the capacity to consent.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy and decision-making is one genuine bioethical concept this source lists, but it is only one of several the source groups together as the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Persons without the capacity to consent is a genuine bioethics topic this source lists, but on its own it omits the other listed concepts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-discrimination and non-stigmatization is a genuine bioethical concept this source lists, but on its own it omits the other listed concepts.
explanations.D: Correct. This source treats autonomy and decision-making, persons without the capacity to consent, non-discrimination and non-stigmatization, and respect for human vulnerability and integrity together as its own umbrella list of core bioethical concepts. None of the individual items alone captures the full list the source marks as correct, so the comprehensive option is the one keyed. This all-of-the-above framing recurs throughout this source whenever it introduces a multi-item list rather than a single fact.

questions.learning_objective: State that bioethical concepts include autonomy and decision making, capacity to consent, non-discrimination and non-stigmatization, and respect for human vulnerability and integrity, together.

questions.title: Medical ethics as a branch of bioethics
questions.question: A branch of bioethics, are simply some key ethical principles that professionals can refer to in the case of any confusion or conflict regarding medical practice. Refer to

explanations.A: Correct. This source names medical ethics as the branch of bioethics that supplies the key ethical principles professionals refer to when medical practice raises confusion or conflict. Medical ethics narrows bioethics' broader ethical, social and legal scope down to the specific principles that guide day-to-day clinical decisions. It is this practical, principle-supplying role that distinguishes medical ethics from bioethics as a whole and from the other options offered.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Medicine is the clinical practice itself, not the branch of bioethics that supplies its guiding ethical principles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Science is a broader category than the specific branch of bioethics the stem describes, and it carries no inherent ethical-principle content.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Love is not a defined branch of bioethics or a source of the professional principles the stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that medical ethics is the branch of bioethics that supplies key principles for resolving confusion or conflict in medical practice.

questions.title: The four principles of medical ethics
questions.question: Principles of medical ethics:

options.A: Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice, together.

explanations.A: Correct. This source lists autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice together as the principles of medical ethics, matching the classical four-principle framework used throughout medical-ethics teaching. Each principle covers a distinct dimension of ethical practice: respecting patient self-determination, acting for the patient's benefit, avoiding harm, and distributing resources fairly. Because the source lists all four together rather than naming any single one as "the" principle, the comprehensive option is the one it keys as correct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Autonomy is one of the four principles, but it alone omits beneficence, non-maleficence and justice, which the source lists together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beneficence is one of the four principles, but it alone omits autonomy, non-maleficence and justice, which the source lists together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The source does name genuine principles of medical ethics, so "none of the above" contradicts the source's own listed content.

questions.learning_objective: State that the principles of medical ethics are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice.

questions.title: Autonomy as self-determination
questions.question: Individual capacity for self-determination, independent decisions, actions, and evaluations. Refer to

explanations.A: Correct. Autonomy is defined here as the individual's capacity for self-determination: making independent decisions, taking independent actions, and forming independent evaluations. This capacity-based definition is distinct from beneficence (acting for another's benefit), non-maleficence (avoiding harm), and justice (fair distribution), each of which describes an obligation toward others rather than a capacity of the individual. It is this self-directed capacity that the stem is naming, which is why autonomy, and not one of the other three principles, is the answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence concerns acting in another person's best interest, not the individual's own capacity for self-determination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm to others, not the individual's own capacity for independent decision-making.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice concerns the fair distribution of resources, not an individual's capacity for self-determination.

questions.learning_objective: State that autonomy is the individual capacity for self-determination, independent decisions, actions, and evaluations.

questions.title: Final word in medical decision making
questions.question: Medical decision making It should be a rational process based on a consideration of the facts, but in the end, the final word is with

explanations.A: Incorrect. This source marks the patient, not the doctor, as holding the final word once the facts have been rationally considered, reflecting the principle of patient autonomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nurse contributes to a patient's care but is not the party this source marks as holding the final decision-making word.
explanations.C: Correct. Even though medical decision-making should be a rational process grounded in a consideration of the facts, this source marks the patient as the one who holds the final word. This reflects the principle of patient autonomy: the physician and care team supply expertise and facts, but the patient's own decision governs what ultimately happens to them. This is consistent with the broader theme, tested elsewhere in this same source, that patients have a right to refuse treatment even when providers disagree.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The family may be involved in some circumstances, but this source marks the patient, not the family, as holding the final word.

questions.learning_objective: State that in medical decision making, the final word rests with the patient.

questions.title: Definition of equality
questions.question: Is state of being equal: having the same rights and social status and aims to ensure that everyone gets the same things to enjoy full, healthy lives. Refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns individual self-determination, not a state of having the same rights and social status as others.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Equity, tested separately in this same source, means identifying and giving people what they specifically need, which differs from equality's same-things-for-everyone framing.
explanations.C: Correct. Equality is defined here as the state of being equal, having the same rights and social status, and aiming to ensure everyone gets the same things to enjoy full, healthy lives. This "same things for everyone" framing is what distinguishes equality from equity, which this source instead defines as giving people what they individually need. The stem's emphasis on sameness of treatment, rather than sameness of outcome through differentiated need, is the key marker of equality specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice, tested separately in this source, concerns fairness in the distribution of resources, not a general state of having the same rights and social status.

questions.learning_objective: State that equality is the state of being equal, having the same rights and social status, so that everyone gets the same things to enjoy full, healthy lives.

questions.title: Definition of equity
questions.question: Trying to identify and give people what they need to enjoy full, healthy lives. Refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns individual self-determination, not identifying and giving people what they need.
explanations.B: Correct. Equity is defined here as trying to identify and give people what they specifically need in order to enjoy full, healthy lives. This need-based, differentiated approach is what distinguishes equity from equality, which this source instead defines as giving everyone the same things regardless of individual need. This distinction is the same one that later underlies vertical and horizontal equity within this same source: treating unequal needs unequally is precisely this need-based idea in practice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equality, tested separately in this source, means giving everyone the same things and the same rights and social status, which differs from equity's need-based framing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice, tested separately in this source, concerns fairness in the distribution of resources broadly, not specifically identifying and meeting individual need.

questions.learning_objective: State that equity is trying to identify and give people what they need to enjoy full, healthy lives.

questions.title: Horizontal equity
questions.question: The equal treatment of equal needs. Refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns individual self-determination, not the equal or unequal treatment of health needs across a population.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vertical equity, tested elsewhere in this module, is the unequal treatment of unequal needs, the opposite pairing from the equal-treatment-of-equal-needs the stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This option's label mixes "horizontal" with "equality" rather than "equity"; the source prints a distinct option using the term "equity" specifically, which is the one it marks correct.
explanations.D: Correct. Horizontal equity is the equal treatment of equal needs: people with the same health needs receive the same care. This is the direct counterpart to vertical equity, which instead calls for unequal (differentiated) treatment of unequal needs, since different social groups have different health needs. Together, horizontal and vertical equity describe the two complementary applications of the equity principle to healthcare need.

questions.learning_objective: State that horizontal equity is the equal treatment of equal needs.

questions.title: Definition of beneficence
questions.question: Actions that promote the wellbeing of others. In the medical context, this means taking actions that serve the best interests of patients. A practitioner should act in the best interest of the patient. The following refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns the patient's own capacity for self-determination, not the practitioner's obligation to promote the patient's wellbeing.
explanations.B: Correct. Beneficence is defined here as taking actions that promote the wellbeing of others, which in the medical context means the practitioner acting in the best interest of the patient and serving their wellbeing. This obligation to actively promote benefit is what distinguishes beneficence from non-maleficence, which is the narrower obligation to avoid causing harm. Both principles are commonly taught as a balanced pair, since a treatment's benefit (beneficence) must be weighed against its risk of harm (non-maleficence).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Competence concerns the intellectual capacity to understand, analyse and judge information, not the obligation to act in a patient's best interest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice concerns the fair distribution of resources, not the practitioner's obligation to promote an individual patient's wellbeing.

questions.learning_objective: State that beneficence is taking actions that promote the wellbeing of others, meaning a practitioner should act in the best interest of the patient.

questions.title: Non-maleficence as "first, do no harm"
questions.question: "First, do no harm," or the Latin, primum non nocere. Many consider that the main or primary consideration should be that: it is more important not to harm your patients than to do them good. Refer to…..

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns the patient's capacity for self-determination, not the obligation to avoid causing harm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence, tested separately in this source, is the obligation to actively promote a patient's wellbeing, the positive counterpart to avoiding harm rather than the avoiding-harm principle itself.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the classic statement of non-maleficence: primum non nocere, "first, do no harm," the view that avoiding harm to a patient takes priority over doing them good. Non-maleficence is often taught alongside beneficence as a balanced pair, since any treatment's risk of harm must be weighed against its potential benefit, but the two remain distinct obligations. The Latin phrasing this stem quotes is the standard citation used across medical-ethics teaching for exactly this principle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice concerns the fair distribution of healthcare resources, not the priority of avoiding harm over doing good.

questions.learning_objective: State that non-maleficence is the principle of "first, do no harm" (primum non nocere): avoiding harm takes priority over doing good.

questions.title: Autonomy requires responsibility
questions.question: There is no autonomy without responsibility.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy is the subject of the aphorism, not the answer it names; the stem is asserting that autonomy depends on this other, separate principle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence concerns acting for a patient's benefit, unrelated to the aphorism linking autonomy and self-accountability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm, unrelated to the aphorism linking autonomy and self-accountability.
explanations.D: Correct. This source keys "there is no autonomy without responsibility" to responsibility itself, the aphorism's point being that the freedom to make independent decisions (autonomy) is inseparable from being answerable for those decisions (responsibility). This mirrors the same source's companion fact that one's awareness of the obligation to decide and act appropriately manifests autonomy. Together these two facts frame autonomy and responsibility as mutually dependent rather than as separate, unrelated principles.

questions.learning_objective: State that there is no autonomy without responsibility.

questions.title: Examination without consent as assault
questions.question: Any physical examination or even blood test without permission or consent from patient is considered an assault except in some cases.

explanations.A: Correct. This source keys this statement to medical consent: performing a physical examination or even a blood test without the patient's permission is treated as an assault, with only limited exceptions (such as emergency lifesaving situations, tested elsewhere in this module). This frames consent as the normal legal and ethical precondition for any physical contact in medical care, not an optional courtesy. The "except in some cases" clause signals that the exceptions themselves are narrow and specifically defined, not a general licence to proceed without consent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence concerns acting in a patient's best interest, not the legal requirement of consent before physical examination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm, not the specific legal requirement of consent before physical contact.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Responsibility concerns being answerable for one's own decisions and actions, not the specific legal requirement of consent before physical examination.

questions.learning_objective: State that medical consent means that a physical examination or blood test performed without permission is considered an assault, except in some defined cases.

questions.title: Invalid consent: operation without medical indication
questions.question: Given consent is considered invalid in the following

options.A: The patient should be sane, above the age of 18, conscious.
options.B: The patient should understand the nature, purpose, and possible complications of treatment.
options.C: Operation without medical indication e.g., amputation of a finger to escape military service.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A sane, adult, conscious patient describes a valid precondition for consent, not a circumstance that invalidates it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Understanding the nature, purpose and possible complications of treatment describes informed consent, a hallmark of valid, not invalid, consent.
explanations.C: Correct. Consent is considered invalid when the operation itself has no medical indication, such as amputating a finger to escape military service. Here the patient may otherwise meet every formal requirement for consent, but the underlying request is not a legitimate medical intervention, which is what invalidates it regardless of the patient's wishes. This example illustrates that valid consent requires a genuine medical purpose behind the procedure, not just the patient's formal agreement to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Being really and freely given describes a hallmark of valid consent, not a circumstance that invalidates it.

questions.learning_objective: State that consent is invalid when it is given for an operation without medical indication, such as amputating a finger to escape military service.

questions.title: Definition of privacy
questions.question: It is the right of an individual or a group to be free from intrusion from others, and includes the right to determine which information about them should be disclosed to others.

options.C: Patients with total impairment of intellectual capacity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Children" is one of the categories of persons without capacity to consent, tested elsewhere in this source, not a definition of the right described here.
explanations.B: Correct. Privacy is defined here as the right of an individual or group to be free from intrusion by others, including the right to determine which information about them should be disclosed. This is a broader right than confidentiality, which specifically concerns an attribute of already-shared personal information not being disclosed further without sufficient reason. Privacy is the individual's own right to control intrusion and disclosure in the first place, before information has necessarily been shared.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Patients with total impairment of intellectual capacity" is one of the categories of persons without capacity to consent, not a definition of the right described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Confidentiality, tested separately in this source, is the narrower attribute of already-disclosed personal information not being shared further, not the individual's general right to be free from intrusion.

questions.learning_objective: State that privacy is the right of an individual or group to be free from intrusion by others, including the right to determine which information about them should be disclosed.

questions.title: Definition of confidentiality
questions.question: An attribute of personal information requiring that it not be disclosed to others without sufficient reason.

options.C: Patients with total impairment of intellectual capacity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Children" is one of the categories of persons without capacity to consent, unrelated to this definition of an attribute of personal information.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Privacy, tested separately in this source, is the individual's broader right to be free from intrusion and to control disclosure, distinct from confidentiality's narrower focus on information already shared.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Patients with total impairment of intellectual capacity" is one of the categories of persons without capacity to consent, unrelated to this definition.
explanations.D: Correct. Confidentiality is defined here as an attribute of personal information: that it should not be disclosed to others without sufficient reason. This is narrower than privacy, which is the individual's general right to be free from intrusion and to control disclosure in the first place. Confidentiality specifically governs what happens to information once it has been shared with a professional, such as a physician, in the course of care.

questions.learning_objective: State that confidentiality is an attribute of personal information requiring that it not be disclosed to others without sufficient reason.

questions.title: Reasons for respecting privacy and confidentiality
questions.question: Reasons for respecting privacy and confidentiality

options.A: Individuals ‘own’ their information: it is essential to their personal integrity.
options.B: For many people privacy is an essential aspect of their dignity; invading their privacy against their will is a violation of their dignity.
options.C: Respect for others requires protecting their privacy and the confidentiality of information about them.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Individuals owning their information as essential to personal integrity is one genuine reason this source lists, but on its own it omits the other reasons listed together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Privacy as essential to dignity is one genuine reason this source lists, but on its own it omits the other reasons listed together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Respect for others requiring protection of privacy and confidentiality is one genuine reason this source lists, but on its own it omits the other reasons listed together.
explanations.D: Correct. This source lists all three reasons together as grounds for respecting privacy and confidentiality: individuals own their information as part of their personal integrity, privacy is essential to personal dignity, and respect for others requires protecting both their privacy and the confidentiality of information about them. None of the three reasons alone captures the complete answer the source marks as correct. This all-of-the-above framing recurs whenever this source introduces a multi-part justification rather than a single fact.

questions.learning_objective: State that reasons for respecting privacy and confidentiality include personal integrity, dignity, and respect for others, together.

questions.title: Definition of vulnerable groups
questions.question: Defined as those at greater risk for poor health status and healthcare access, experience significant disparities in access to and use of healthcare services. They are more likely to develop health problems as a result of exposure to risk.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Integrity is not the term this source keys to this description of groups facing poor health status and access disparities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vulnerability, tested separately in this source, is the underlying susceptibility to stressors, the trait, rather than the specific groups who experience the resulting health-access disparities described here.
explanations.C: Correct. Vulnerable groups are defined here as those at greater risk for poor health status and healthcare access, who experience significant disparities in access to and use of healthcare services, and who are more likely to develop health problems from exposure to risk. This is the population-level, group-focused counterpart to vulnerability, which this source defines as the underlying susceptibility itself. Vulnerable groups are the people; vulnerability is the trait that puts them at risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Habits" is not the term this source keys to this description of a population facing health-access disparities.

questions.learning_objective: State that vulnerable groups are those at greater risk for poor health status and healthcare access, experiencing significant disparities and more likely to develop health problems from exposure to risk.

questions.title: Definition of vulnerability
questions.question: Is susceptibility to actual or potential stressors that may lead to adverse effects.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Integrity is not the term this source keys to this definition of susceptibility to stressors.
explanations.B: Correct. Vulnerability is defined here as susceptibility to actual or potential stressors that may lead to adverse effects. This is the underlying trait or state, distinct from vulnerable groups, which this source defines as the specific populations who experience poor health status and access disparities as a result of that susceptibility. Understanding vulnerability as a susceptibility, rather than as the population itself, is what lets this source separately test the causes of vulnerability (biological, environmental, social) as a distinct fact.

questions.title: Ancillary team example: cleaners and domestic staff
questions.question: Cleaners & domestic staff are considered

explanations.A: Incorrect. The core (care) team is formed of members directly involved in caring for patients, not the indirect domestic support this stem describes.
explanations.B: Correct. This source classifies cleaners and domestic staff specifically as the ancillary team. This is the named example the source gives for the ancillary team type, which this module elsewhere defines in general terms as support services providing indirect, task-specific services in a health care facility. Cleaners and domestic staff support the facility's operation without directly delivering patient care, which is exactly the ancillary role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Support services" is this source's general term for indirect task-specific services, but the specific option this source keys for cleaners and domestic staff by name is "ancillary team."
explanations.D: Incorrect. A contingency team deals with emergencies and specific events such as a cardiac arrest, not the routine domestic support cleaners and domestic staff provide.

questions.learning_objective: State that cleaners and domestic staff are considered the ancillary team.

questions.title: Forming stage: ambiguity and confusion
questions.question: Stage of team dynamic which is characterized by ambiguity & confusion is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Storming is characterised by conflict and rebellion against assigned tasks once roles are already somewhat clear, not the initial ambiguity and confusion this stem describes.
explanations.B: Correct. Forming is the stage of team development this source characterises by ambiguity and confusion, as team members are still unclear about their tasks. This is the first stage of the classic team-development sequence, before storming's conflict, norming's open communication and task engagement, and performing's full focus on achieving goals. Recognising forming as the ambiguity-and-confusion stage, rather than storming's conflict, is the specific distinction this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Performing is the stage where the team focuses all its attention on achieving goals, the most resolved stage, not the initial ambiguity this stem describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Norming is the stage of open communication where the team starts to confront the task at hand, a later, more resolved stage than the initial ambiguity this stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that forming is the stage of team dynamics characterized by ambiguity and confusion.

questions.title: Norming stage: open communication
questions.question: In which stage of team dynamic, team members has open communication & starts to confront the task at hand

explanations.A: Incorrect. Storming is characterised by conflict and rebellion against assigned tasks, not the open communication and task-confronting this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Forming is characterised by ambiguity and confusion about tasks, the opposite of the open communication this stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Performing is the stage where the team focuses all its attention on achieving goals, a further stage beyond the open communication this stem describes.
explanations.D: Correct. Norming is the stage of team dynamics this source defines by open communication between team members, who start to confront the task at hand as procedures become accepted and communication patterns are established. This follows storming's conflict and precedes performing's full focus on goal achievement, marking the point where the team moves from disagreement toward functional collaboration.

questions.learning_objective: State that norming is the stage of team dynamics with open communication, where team members start to confront the task at hand.

questions.title: Unmodifiable determinants (exception)
questions.question: Un-modifiable determinants: (Biological factors): except

explanations.A: Incorrect. Genetic factors are a genuine unmodifiable biological determinant this source lists, so this option is not the exception being asked for.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gender is a genuine unmodifiable biological determinant this source lists, so this option is not the exception being asked for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Age and ageing of the population is a genuine unmodifiable biological determinant this source lists, so this option is not the exception being asked for.
explanations.D: Correct. This source lists genetic factors, gender, and age and ageing of the population together as unmodifiable biological determinants of health, and marks behavioural and socio-cultural factors as the exception, since these are modifiable rather than fixed. This pairs directly with this source's companion list of modifiable determinants, which instead names health services, physical environment, social support networks and political system as modifiable, with gender marked there as its own exception since it does not change. Recognising which determinants a source treats as fixed versus changeable is the point of this "except" framing.

questions.learning_objective: State that genetic factors, gender, and age and ageing of the population are unmodifiable biological determinants of health; behavioural and socio-cultural factors are the exception.

questions.title: Socio-economic factors
questions.question: Socio-economic factors: like:

options.D: Income and social class, education, and occupation, all together.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Income and social class is one genuine socio-economic factor this source lists, but alone it omits the other factors the source groups together as the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Education is one genuine socio-economic factor this source lists, but alone it omits the other factors the source groups together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Occupation is one genuine socio-economic factor this source lists, but alone it omits the other factors the source groups together.
explanations.D: Correct. This source lists income and social class, education, and occupation together as its named socio-economic factors affecting health. These sit within the broader modifiable-determinants framework this source tests elsewhere, since socio-economic circumstances can change over a lifetime, unlike the fixed biological factors such as genetics, gender and age. None of the three factors alone captures the complete socio-economic category the source marks as correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that socio-economic factors include income and social class, education, and occupation, together.

questions.title: Physical environment as a health determinant
questions.question: Safe water and clean air, healthy workplaces, safe houses, communities, and roads all contribute to good health.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Health services, tested separately in this source, concern access to and use of preventive and treatment services, not the physical surroundings this stem describes.
explanations.B: Correct. Physical environment is the determinant this source defines through the examples of safe water and clean air, healthy workplaces, safe houses, communities and roads, all of which contribute to good health. This is one of the modifiable determinants of health this source lists, alongside health services, social support networks and political system, distinguished from the unmodifiable biological factors such as genetics, gender and age.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Social support networks concern relationships and community connection, not the physical surroundings such as water, air, housing and roads this stem describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Political system concerns governance and policy structures, not the physical surroundings such as water, air, housing and roads this stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that physical environment, e.g. safe water and clean air, healthy workplaces, safe houses, communities, and roads, contributes to good health.

questions.title: Health services as a health determinant
questions.question: Access and use of services that prevent and treat diseases influence health

explanations.A: Correct. Health services is the determinant this source defines as the access to and use of services that prevent and treat disease, which in turn influences health. This is one of the modifiable determinants of health this source lists, alongside physical environment, social support networks and political system, distinguished from the fixed biological factors such as genetics, gender and age tested elsewhere in this module.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Physical environment, tested separately in this source, concerns surroundings such as safe water, air, housing and roads, not access to and use of preventive and treatment services.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Social support networks concern relationships and community connection, not access to and use of preventive and treatment services.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Political system concerns governance and policy structures, not access to and use of preventive and treatment services.

questions.learning_objective: State that health services, meaning access to and use of services that prevent and treat diseases, influence health.

questions.title: Definition of lifestyle
questions.question: Lifestyle is composed of cultural, behavioural pattern and lifelong personal habits developed through socialization.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Health services concern access to and use of preventive and treatment services, not the cultural and behavioural pattern this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Physical environment concerns surroundings such as safe water, air, housing and roads, not the cultural and behavioural pattern this stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Social support networks concern relationships and community connection, not the cultural and behavioural pattern this stem describes.
explanations.D: Correct. Lifestyle is defined here as being composed of cultural, behavioural pattern and lifelong personal habits developed through socialization, and this source keys it to behavioural and socio-cultural factors. This is the same category this source elsewhere marks as the exception to the fixed, unmodifiable biological determinants (genetic factors, gender, age), since lifestyle habits, unlike genetics or age, can change over a lifetime through socialization and personal choice.

questions.learning_objective: State that lifestyle is composed of cultural, behavioural pattern and lifelong personal habits developed through socialization, classified as a behavioural and socio-cultural factor.
